'''''Iris ensata''''', the '''Japanese iris'''<ref>Rudy J. Favretti and Joy P. Favretti {{Googlebooks|I9LR1XuKjMIC|Landscapes and Gardens for Historic Buildings: A Handbook for Reproducing and creating authentic landscape settings|page=145}}</ref> or '''Japanese water iris''' ([[Japanese language|Japanese]]: '''''hanashōbu''''', ハナショウブ), formerly ''I. kaempferi'', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family Iridaceae, native to [[Japan]], [[China]], [[Korea]] and [[Russia]], and widely cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]]. "[[Japanese iris]]" may also refer to ''[[Iris sanguinea|I. sanguinea]]'' and ''[[Iris laevigata|I. laevigata]]'', both native to Japan.

==Description==
''Iris ensata'' is an erect [[rhizome|rhizomatous]] [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] growing to {{convert|80|cm|in|abbr=on}} tall, with strap-shaped leaves. The flower, appearing in midsummer, is purple with a flash of yellow on the falls.<ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/9240/i-Iris-ensata-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Iris ensata'' | accessdate = 14 March 2018}}</ref> The bluish purple color of the flowers is an example of the [[copigmentation]] phenomenon.<ref>Anthocyanin-flavone copigmentation in bluish purple flowers of Japanese garden iris (Iris ensata Thunb.) T. Yabuya, M. Nakamura, T. Iwashina, M. Yamaguchi and T. Takehara, EUPHYTICA, Volume 98, Number 3, 163–167, {{doi|10.1023/A:1003152813333}}</ref>

==Habitat==
Widely distributed throughout the Japanese archipelago and elsewhere, ''I. ensata'' is very hardy down to {{convert|-20 |C|F|abbr=on}}. It prefers a boggy or marshy environment and soil with a low (acidic) [[soil pH|pH]]. In favourable conditions it will eventually form sizable clumps.

==Cultivation==
''Iris ensata'' is extensively grown as an [[ornamental plant]] in [[Garden|gardens]] and [[Park|parks]] throughout the [[temperateness|temperate zones]] of the world.

''Iris ensata'' is highly prized in Japan. It is possible that it was introduced into Japanese culture in [[Ancient history|ancient times]], in association with [[Rice|rice farming]].<ref name = Marwood/> Certainly it has been cultivated and [[Orbital hybridisation|hybridised]] there for at least five centuries. The {{Nihongo|''hanashōbu''|ハナショウブ, 花菖蒲||extra={{ill|Iris ensata var. ensata|ja|ハナショウブ|italics=y}}, syn. ''I. ensata'' var. ''hortensis'', ''I. kaempferi''}} grows in the wet land and is the most extensively cultivated variety in Japanese gardens. According to the place where it was cultivated, ''I. ensata'' is classified into three strains – the Edo (Tokyo), Higo (Kumamoto Prefecture) and Ise (Mie Prefecture).

Upon being introduced to the west in the mid-19th century, a new chapter was opened in the cultivation of this species. In America it was intensively hybridised to produce many new cultivars. Perhaps the most influential breeders in the United States have been Arlie Payne of Indiana, the Marx family of Oregon, Arthur Hazzard of Michigan, and Currier McEwan of Maine. Between them they have produced plants with large blooms and a wide range of colours. In the UK interest in this plant has been equally strong.
